\chapter{Hablo --- One Form, Two Readings}
\label{ch:hablo-dos}
\hlchaptermodality{257}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use the plain present for both a habit and this moment.}

I can use the plain present for both a habit and this moment.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hablo]{hablo — one form, two readings}

\label{lesson:ES-C66-hablo-dos-lecturas}



\begin{quote}
Somebody phones and asks what you are doing. Answer with \emph{comer}, in the present, without using the \emph{-iendo} form.

You said \emph{como}. Now think about what that sentence actually claimed.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it was doing both all along}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{Como.} — I eat. \textbf{And also}: I'm eating, right now, this minute.
\end{quote}

One form, two readings. The \textbf{durative} one is the habit — \emph{I eat at eight}. The \textbf{actual} one is this moment — \emph{I'm eating, don't ring back}. English keeps two shapes; Spanish keeps one.

You have been using both since the very first verb, without anybody naming either.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Which raises the obvious question about the form you learned nineteen chapters ago. If \emph{como} already means \emph{I'm eating}, what is \emph{estoy comiendo} for?

\textbf{Insistence.} The progressive is not the ordinary way to say what you are doing now — it is the way to say it when the \emph{now} is the point.

\begin{quote}
— \emph{¿Qué haces?} — \emph{Como.} (perfectly normal) — \emph{¡Estoy comiendo!} — I'm \textbf{in the middle of eating}, leave me alone.
\end{quote}

So the progressive is \textbf{optional} where English's is compulsory. An English speaker reaches for \emph{estoy comiendo} every time and sounds oddly emphatic; a Spanish speaker uses the plain present and saves the long form for when it means something.

This is worth more than it looks. It means you already had a complete present tense before that chapter, and the progressive was an addition rather than a repair.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{Como} as an answer, then \emph{Estoy comiendo} as a protest
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many readings does the plain present carry? (\textbf{Two} — the habit and this moment.)

And is the progressive required for \emph{right now}? (\textbf{No.} It is for insisting.)
\end{tcolorbox}
